articles.title: Snapchat joins other popular platforms in fight against 'AI slop'
articles.summary: Snapchat, YouTube, LinkedIn, and Substack are trying to combat the proliferation of fake AI content.
articles.content:
As Chris Best, the co-founder and chief executive of Substack put it last week: "It's getting harder to tell what's real on the internet."

Announcing a new tool, external designed to let readers on the newsletter platform detect AI-generated writing, Best cited other research that has found up to 40% of writing on social media is now fake or AI-generated.

"Platforms that reward fakeness will create a race to the bottom," Best said.

LinkedIn, a social media platform focused on work, introduced a button on its platform this week that allows any user to report if a post or a comment appears to be AI-generated.

"AI slop is a top priority for all of us," LinkedIn's chief product officer Hari Srinivasan wrote on the platform.

In just the last couple of months, he said the platform had "blocked billions" of attempts to post AI-generated comments.

"Every day we are now catching hundreds of thousands of automated comment attempts," Srinivasan said.

Like Snap, LinkedIn said it is not rejecting the use of AI entirely and users that use AI tools to "refine" their posts should not get caught up in efforts to combat AI slop.

Nonetheless, LinkedIn is removing an automated prompt that would show up for users writing a post offering to "enhance" it through the use of AI. It will go back to a simple proofreading tool.

YouTube, the video platform owned by Google, also this month updated its policies, external around what kind of content can be monetised by creators.

Research from last year found scores of channels on YouTube that were solely AI-generated content, external, many of which had millions of subscribers and some of which made millions of dollars in revenue.

In an effort to discourage YouTube from filling up with what the platform calls "inauthentic content", earlier this month the site broke down into three categories the kind of videos that will not be allowed to make money through it: generic, repetitive, or template-based.

Those styles of content are much easier to make, and quickly, with the use of generative AI tools.

YouTube's trust and safety chief Matt Halprin said in an interview, external on the updated rules that, while AI tools can help people with their content, they are more frequently being used to create fake and low-quality videos.

"The same technology really enables great stuff," Halprin said.

"But it also enables stuff that's kind of content farming, and that's the stuff that we don't want to have."

articles.personality_title: Major platforms take steps to fight fake AI content online
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many social media sites are seeing more fake or AI-made content that can trick people. This makes it hard to know what is real on the internet.

**What happened** – Snapchat, YouTube, LinkedIn, and Substack have started new actions to stop fake AI content. For example, Substack created a tool to help readers spot AI-written newsletters. LinkedIn added a button so users can report posts or comments that seem AI-generated. YouTube updated its rules to stop certain easy-to-make AI videos from earning money.

**Impact** – These steps are important because a lot of online writing and videos are now fake or made by AI. LinkedIn said it blocks billions of fake AI comments every few months. YouTube wants to keep videos real and interesting, not just made quickly by AI. This helps people trust what they see and read online.

**What's next step** – Platforms will keep improving their tools to find and stop fake AI content. Users may see fewer fake posts and videos, and more clear ways to report suspicious content. This effort might also push creators to make more original and honest content.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Leading social media sites are actively working to reduce fake AI content, helping users find more trustworthy information online.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les grandes plateformes luttent contre les contenus IA faux en ligne
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux sites de réseaux sociaux voient de plus en plus de contenus faux ou créés par IA, ce qui rend difficile de savoir ce qui est vrai sur internet.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Snapchat, YouTube, LinkedIn et Substack ont lancé de nouvelles actions pour stopper ces contenus IA faux. Par exemple, Substack a créé un outil pour aider les lecteurs à détecter les newsletters écrites par IA. LinkedIn a ajouté un bouton pour que les utilisateurs signalent les publications ou commentaires qui semblent générés par IA. YouTube a mis à jour ses règles pour empêcher certains vidéos faciles à faire par IA de gagner de l'argent.

**Impact** – Ces mesures sont importantes car beaucoup d’écrits et vidéos en ligne sont maintenant faux ou créés par IA. LinkedIn bloque des milliards de faux commentaires IA tous les quelques mois. YouTube veut garder des vidéos vraies et intéressantes, pas juste faites rapidement par IA. Cela aide les gens à avoir confiance dans ce qu'ils voient et lisent en ligne.

**Prochaine étape** – Les plateformes vont continuer à améliorer leurs outils pour détecter et arrêter les contenus IA faux. Les utilisateurs verront peut-être moins de posts et vidéos faux, et auront plus de moyens pour signaler les contenus suspects. Cet effort pourrait aussi encourager les créateurs à produire des contenus plus originaux et honnêtes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les principaux sites de réseaux sociaux travaillent activement à réduire les contenus IA faux pour aider les utilisateurs à trouver des informations plus fiables en ligne.
articles.personality_title_es: Grandes plataformas luchan contra contenido falso generado por IA en línea
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas redes sociales están viendo más contenido falso o creado por IA, lo que dificulta saber qué es real en internet.

**Qué pasó** – Snapchat, YouTube, LinkedIn y Substack empezaron nuevas acciones para detener el contenido falso generado por IA. Por ejemplo, Substack creó una herramienta para ayudar a los lectores a detectar boletines escritos por IA. LinkedIn agregó un botón para que los usuarios reporten publicaciones o comentarios que parezcan generados por IA. YouTube actualizó sus reglas para evitar que ciertos videos fáciles de hacer con IA ganen dinero.

**Impacto** – Estas medidas son importantes porque muchos escritos y videos en línea ahora son falsos o hechos por IA. LinkedIn bloquea miles de millones de comentarios falsos de IA cada pocos meses. YouTube quiere mantener videos reales e interesantes, no solo hechos rápido por IA. Esto ayuda a las personas a confiar en lo que ven y leen en línea.

**Próximo paso** – Las plataformas seguirán mejorando sus herramientas para encontrar y detener contenido falso generado por IA. Los usuarios podrían ver menos publicaciones y videos falsos, y tener más formas de reportar contenido sospechoso. Esto también podría motivar a los creadores a hacer contenido más original y honesto.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las principales redes sociales están trabajando activamente para reducir el contenido falso generado por IA y ayudar a los usuarios a encontrar información más confiable en línea.
